source_quote: Because the palmar cutaneous nerve takes its origin proximal to the wrist joint, the sensation on the thenar eminence and proximal radial palm is spared.
vignette: A 45-year-old typist reports numbness and tingling in the right thumb, index, and middle fingers that awakens her from sleep. Shaking her hand provides temporary relief. Examination demonstrates weakness and wasting of the abductor pollicis brevis muscle. Tapping over the volar wrist reproduces paresthesias in the radial three-and-a-half digits. Sensation over the thenar eminence is entirely normal.
question: Why is sensation over the thenar eminence preserved despite severe carpal tunnel syndrome?
options: The thenar eminence is innervated exclusively by the superficial branch of the radial nerve
The anterior interosseous nerve supplies sensation to the base of the thumb
The recurrent motor branch of the median nerve carries all thenar sensory fibers
The palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve branches proximal to the flexor retinaculum and passes superficial to the carpal tunnel
Sensory fibers to the thenar eminence are spared within the deepest fascicles of the carpal tunnel

explanation.why_correct: The palmar cutaneous branch arises from the median nerve approximately 5 cm proximal to the wrist and travels superficial to the flexor retinaculum (transverse carpal ligament). Consequently, it is spared in carpal tunnel compression, preserving sensation over the thenar eminence. Sensory loss extending onto the thenar eminence indicates a more proximal lesion (such as pronator teres syndrome or C6 radiculopathy).
distractors: The superficial radial nerve supplies the dorsum of the thumb and first web space, not the volar thenar eminence.
The anterior interosseous nerve is a pure motor nerve supplying deep forearm muscles and the wrist joint capsule, with no cutaneous sensory distribution.
The recurrent motor branch supplies thenar muscles (LOAF: Lumbricals 1-2, APB, OP, FPB superficial head) and has no cutaneous sensory innervation.
Thenar sensory fibers do not run inside the carpal tunnel; their sparing is anatomical due to superficial routing.
explanation.key_point: Sparing of thenar eminence sensation differentiates carpal tunnel syndrome from proximal median nerve lesions (pronator syndrome) and C6 radiculopathy.

source_quote: pinch attitude of the hand while attempting to make a full circle by applying the pulp of the thumb to that of the index finger
vignette: A 32-year-old tennis player develops deep proximal forearm pain followed by difficulty pinching small objects. On examination, when asked to make an 'OK' sign with the thumb and index finger, the patient pinches using extended terminal phalanges (pulp-to-pulp contact) rather than flexing the distal interphalangeal joints (tip-to-tip contact). Cutaneous sensory examination across the entire hand and arm is completely normal.
question: Which nerve and muscles are specifically impaired in this condition?
options: Posterior interosseous nerve impairing extensor pollicis longus and extensor digitorum
Recurrent motor branch of the median nerve impairing abductor pollicis brevis
Anterior interosseous nerve impairing flexor pollicis longus and flexor digitorum profundus to the index finger
Deep branch of the ulnar nerve impairing first dorsal interosseous and adductor pollicis
Musculocutaneous nerve impairing the brachialis muscle

explanation.why_correct: The patient exhibits the classic Kiloh-Nevin syndrome (anterior interosseous nerve syndrome). The AIN is a pure motor branch of the median nerve supplying the flexor pollicis longus (flexion of thumb interphalangeal joint), the radial half of the flexor digitorum profundus (flexion of index and middle DIP joints), and the pronator quadratus. Inability to flex the thumb IP and index DIP joints prevents forming a normal tip-to-tip circle, causing the pathognomonic flat pinch ('pulp-to-pulp' pinch) without any sensory loss.
distractors: Posterior interosseous nerve palsy causes weakness of finger and thumb extension (finger drop), not distal flexion.
Recurrent motor median palsy impairs thumb abduction and opposition, but DIP and IP flexion are preserved.
Deep ulnar nerve lesion produces Froment sign and interosseous weakness, but does not prevent tip-to-tip flexion of the thumb IP and index DIP.
Musculocutaneous nerve innervates biceps and coracobrachialis, with sensory loss along the lateral forearm via the lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerve.
explanation.key_point: Anterior interosseous neuropathy (Kiloh-Nevin) produces failure of the 'OK' sign (pulp-to-pulp pinch) due to weak FPL and radial FDP without sensory loss.

section: Ulnar Nerve Entrapment: Elbow vs Wrist
vignette: A 56-year-old cyclist presents with numbness in the little finger and hypothenar wasting of the right hand. Sensory examination confirms dense sensory loss on the palmar surface of the little finger and hypothenar eminence, but pinprick sensation on the dorsal ulnar aspect of the hand is entirely intact. Motor examination demonstrates weakness of the interossei and adductor pollicis with mild clawing of the fourth and fifth digits, while flexor carpi ulnaris strength is normal.
question: Where is the ulnar nerve lesion localized?
options: Cubital tunnel behind the medial epicondyle
Cervical spinal nerve root C8
Medial cord of the brachial plexus
Thoracic outlet with compression by a cervical rib
Ulnar canal at the wrist (Guyon canal)

explanation.why_correct: The dorsal ulnar cutaneous branch arises 5 to 8 cm proximal to the wrist and travels superficially to innervate the dorsoulnar hand. In lesions at or distal to the wrist within Guyon canal, this dorsal branch is spared, leaving dorsal ulnar hand sensation intact while palmar ulnar sensation is impaired. In contrast, lesions at the elbow (cubital tunnel) produce sensory loss on both the palmar and dorsal surfaces of the ulnar hand and usually weaken the flexor carpi ulnaris and medial flexor digitorum profundus.
distractors: Cubital tunnel lesions impair sensation on the dorsal ulnar hand because the lesion is proximal to the takeoff of the dorsal cutaneous branch.
C8 radiculopathy produces sensory loss that extends proximally into the medial forearm and impairs C8-innervated median muscles (FPL, APB).
Medial cord lesions involve median-innervated C8-T1 muscles (thenar muscles) and cause medial antebrachial cutaneous sensory loss.
Thoracic outlet syndrome characteristically causes prominent thenar wasting (C8-T1 fibers via median nerve) and medial arm/forearm sensory loss.
explanation.key_point: Sparing of dorsal ulnar hand sensation differentiates ulnar nerve entrapment at Guyon canal (wrist) from cubital tunnel syndrome (elbow).

section: Radial Nerve Lesions: Spiral Groove vs Axilla vs PIN
source_quote: The triceps muscle (and therefore the triceps reflex) is spared because the branches to the muscle have a proximal origin.
vignette: A 48-year-old man awakens after falling asleep with his arm draped over the back of a wooden chair following heavy alcohol consumption. He cannot extend his wrist or fingers on the right side. On examination, there is wrist drop and finger drop. The brachioradialis muscle is weak, and there is numbness over the dorsal first web space. However, elbow extension against resistance is completely normal with a brisk, symmetrical triceps reflex.
question: Where is the radial nerve lesion localized?
options: Spiral (radial) groove of the humerus
Axilla (proximal to branches to the triceps)
Supinator muscle (arcade of Fröhse) affecting the posterior interosseous nerve
Posterior cord of the brachial plexus
C7 spinal nerve root

explanation.why_correct: Compression at the spiral groove (Saturday night palsy) damages the radial nerve after the branches to the triceps muscle have already exited in the axilla. Therefore, triceps strength and the triceps reflex are intact, while muscles innervated distally (brachioradialis, extensor carpi radialis longus, and all PIN-innervated extensors) are paralyzed, along with numbness over the superficial radial sensory distribution.
distractors: Axillary radial compression impairs elbow extension and abolishes the triceps reflex because branches to the triceps arise in the axilla.
Posterior interosseous nerve (PIN) entrapment at the arcade of Fröhse produces pure finger and thumb drop without wrist drop (ECRL is spared) and has zero sensory loss.
Posterior cord plexopathy involves the axillary nerve (deltoid weakness) and thoracodorsal nerve (latissimus dorsi weakness) as well as the triceps.
C7 radiculopathy impairs the triceps reflex and elbow extension, but spares the brachioradialis (C5-C6).
explanation.key_point: Radial nerve compression at the spiral groove spares the triceps and triceps reflex while causing wrist drop, finger drop, and dorsal web space numbness.

vignette: A 62-year-old man who recently lost 15 kg develops a left foot drop. Examination demonstrates marked weakness of ankle dorsiflexion and ankle eversion. Sensation is decreased over the lateral lower leg and dorsum of the foot. Ankle inversion is completely normal, and the patellar and Achilles reflexes are symmetrical and intact.
question: What anatomical distinction confirms common fibular (peroneal) neuropathy at the fibular head over an L5 radiculopathy?
options: Preservation of ankle eversion (fibularis longus muscle innervated by the superficial fibular nerve)
Absence of sensory loss over the first dorsal web space
Sparing of the extensor hallucis longus muscle
Preservation of ankle inversion (tibialis posterior muscle innervated by the tibial nerve)
Loss of the Achilles tendon reflex

explanation.why_correct: The tibialis posterior muscle inverts the foot and is innervated by the tibial nerve (L5). In a common fibular (peroneal) neuropathy at the fibular head, eversion and dorsiflexion are weak, but foot inversion is completely preserved. In an L5 radiculopathy, both the fibular muscles (eversion) AND the tibialis posterior (inversion) are weak. Preserved inversion definitively localizes the foot drop to the fibular nerve.
distractors: Ankle eversion is weak in fibular neuropathy because the superficial fibular nerve is damaged at the fibular head.
The first web space is supplied by the deep fibular nerve and is typically numb in common fibular neuropathy.
Extensor hallucis longus is innervated by the deep fibular nerve and is profoundly weak in fibular neuropathy.
The Achilles reflex is mediated by S1 via the tibial nerve; it is intact in both fibular neuropathy and L5 radiculopathy.
explanation.key_point: Normal foot inversion (tibialis posterior, tibial nerve) distinguishes common fibular neuropathy at the fibular head from an L5 radiculopathy.

source_quote: The triceps muscle (and therefore the triceps reflex) is spared because the branches to the muscle have a proximal origin.
vignette: A 28-year-old man awakens after a deep alcohol-induced sleep with his arm draped over a hard chair. He cannot extend his wrist or fingers, causing prominent wrist drop. The brachioradialis reflex is absent, and he has numbness over the first dorsal web space, but his triceps strength and triceps reflex are completely normal.
question: Where is the radial nerve compressed?
options: Axilla, proximal to the radial nerve branch to the triceps muscle
Spiral (radial) groove of the humerus, distal to the branch to the triceps
Supinator muscle canal (arcade of Frohse) affecting the posterior interosseous nerve
Anatomic snuffbox affecting the superficial sensory radial nerve branch

explanation.why_correct: Compression at the humeral spiral groove ('Saturday night palsy') spares the triceps branch (which arises proximally in the axilla) but paralyses the brachioradialis, wrist extensors, and finger extensors, with numbness over the dorsal first web space.
distractors: Axillary compression (e.g. crutch palsy) affects the triceps, causing inability to extend the elbow with loss of the triceps jerk.
Posterior interosseous nerve compression at the arcade of Frohse causes finger drop without sensory deficit or brachioradialis weakness.
Superficial radial sensory entrapment (cheiralgia paresthetica) produces isolated sensory symptoms without any motor weakness.
explanation.key_point: Radial neuropathy at the spiral groove causes wrist and finger drop with brachioradialis weakness, but uniquely spares triceps extension.

vignette: A 54-year-old cyclist reports tingling and numbness in his right little finger and medial half of the ring finger. Examination shows weakness of the abductor digiti minimi and first dorsal interosseous, with a positive Froment sign. Sensation over the dorsal medial aspect of the hand is completely normal, and sensation over the hypothenar palm is also normal.
question: Where is the ulnar nerve lesion located?
options: Retrocondylar groove of the elbow behind the medial epicondyle
Deep palmar motor branch of the ulnar nerve in Guyon canal (Zone II)
Cubital tunnel beneath the aponeurotic arch of flexor carpi ulnaris
Lower trunk of the brachial plexus in the scalene triangle

explanation.why_correct: The deep motor branch in Guyon canal spares the dorsal cutaneous branch (which branches in the forearm) and the palmar sensory branch, producing motor weakness of intrinsic hand muscles without dorsal hand sensory loss.
distractors: Elbow lesions at the retrocondylar groove or cubital tunnel cause sensory loss over the dorsal medial hand due to involvement of the dorsal ulnar cutaneous nerve.
Cubital tunnel syndrome typically presents with sensory symptoms in the medial hand and flexor carpi ulnaris involvement.
Lower trunk brachial plexopathy causes weakness of all C8-T1 muscles (including median-innervated thenar muscles) and Horner syndrome.
explanation.key_point: Normal sensation over the dorsal medial hand rules out an elbow ulnar neuropathy, localizing the lesion to Guyon's canal at the wrist.

vignette: A 42-year-old woman presents with acute right foot drop after wearing tight leg casts. Examination shows weak foot dorsiflexion (tibialis anterior 1/5) and foot eversion (peroneus longus 2/5). However, foot inversion (tibialis posterior) and ankle jerk reflex are completely normal.
question: Which localization is confirmed by the preservation of foot inversion?
options: Common fibular (peroneal) nerve at the fibular head
L5 nerve root radiculopathy
Sciatic nerve trunk in the piriformis canal
Tibial nerve in the popliteal fossa

explanation.why_correct: The tibialis posterior muscle (foot inversion) is innervated by the tibial nerve (L5). A common fibular neuropathy impairs dorsiflexion and eversion but spares inversion. An L5 radiculopathy impairs both dorsiflexion AND inversion.
distractors: L5 radiculopathy causes weakness of both foot dorsiflexion and foot inversion (tibialis posterior), distinguishing it from fibular neuropathy.
Sciatic nerve trunk injury affects both fibular and tibial branches, causing weak inversion and impaired ankle jerk.
Tibial nerve injury paralyzes plantar flexion and inversion, leaving dorsiflexion intact.
explanation.key_point: Preserved foot inversion (tibialis posterior) is the cardinal clinical sign distinguishing a common fibular nerve lesion from an L5 radiculopathy.

source_quote: Compression or angulation of the nerve by the inguinal ligament near the anterior superior iliac spine may result in acute or subacute pain and paresthesias
vignette: A 48-year-old obese police officer wearing a heavy duty belt reports burning dysesthesias and numbness over the anterolateral right thigh. Sensory testing reveals hypoesthesia strictly limited to the lateral thigh, with normal quadriceps strength and normal patellar reflex.
question: What is the diagnosis?
options: Femoral neuropathy caused by retroperitoneal hematoma
L2–L3 radiculopathy from disc herniation
Obturator neuropathy compressed in the obturator canal
Meralgia paresthetica (entrapment of the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve under the inguinal ligament)

explanation.why_correct: The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve (L2–L3) is a purely sensory nerve. Entrapment under the inguinal ligament (meralgia paresthetica) produces burning pain over the anterolateral thigh with completely normal motor exam and knee jerk.
distractors: Femoral neuropathy causes quadriceps weakness, thigh wasting, and an absent patellar reflex.
L2-L3 radiculopathy involves motor weakness (hip flexion/knee extension) and dermatomal pain radiating across the anterior thigh.
Obturator neuropathy causes pain and weakness in the medial thigh adductors, not the lateral thigh.
explanation.key_point: Meralgia paresthetica is a pure sensory syndrome of the anterolateral thigh with strictly normal motor power and preserved patellar reflex.

source_quote: pinch attitude of the hand while attempting to make a full circle by applying the pulp of the thumb to that of the index finger
vignette: A 32-year-old violinist presents with difficulty writing and buttoning shirts. On examination, when asked to make an 'OK' sign with thumb and index finger, she forms a pinch sign with extended distal phalanges ('pad-to-pad' instead of 'tip-to-tip'). Sensation across the entire hand is completely intact.
question: Which nerve branch is selectively compromised?
options: Anterior interosseous nerve (Kiloh-Nevin syndrome)
Recurrent thenar motor branch of the median nerve at the flexor retinaculum
Main trunk of the median nerve within the carpal tunnel
Deep motor branch of the ulnar nerve at the hook of hamate

explanation.why_correct: The anterior interosseous nerve (AIN) is a purely motor branch of the median nerve supplying the flexor pollicis longus (FPL), flexor digitorum profundus (FDP) I & II, and pronator quadratus. Inability to flex the distal thumb and index phalanges prevents a round 'OK' sign, with no sensory loss.
distractors: The recurrent motor branch supplies the abductor pollicis brevis, opponens pollicis, and superficial FPB; its lesion weakens thumb abduction, not distal flexion.
Carpal tunnel syndrome causes paresthesias in the thumb, index, and middle fingers with sensory loss over the lateral palm.
Deep ulnar motor branch paralysis impairs the first dorsal interosseous and adductor pollicis, causing a positive Froment sign, not an abnormal 'OK' pinch.
explanation.key_point: Anterior interosseous neuropathy (Kiloh-Nevin syndrome) produces pure motor failure of FPL and FDP index, collapsing the 'OK' sign into a flat pinch without sensory loss.

section: Ulnar nerve lesions at the wrist
source_quote: there is sensory loss on the distal palm and the palmar surfaces of the fifth finger and the medial half of the fourth finger
vignette: A 52-year-old woman has weakness of all the intrinsic hand muscles supplied by the ulnar nerve. Imaging shows a carpal ganglion compressing the ulnar nerve as it enters the hand, just proximal to the origin of the superficial terminal sensory branch and distal to the palmar and dorsal cutaneous branches.
question: Which sensory deficit is expected?
options: Loss on both the palmar and dorsal surfaces of the fifth finger and ulnar half of the fourth finger, extending over the ulnar hand to the wrist
Loss limited to the dorsum of the ulnar hand and the dorsal surface of the fifth finger
No sensory loss, because only motor fibers are compressed
Loss on the distal palm and palmar surfaces of the fifth finger and medial half of the fourth finger, with the proximal palm and entire dorsum of the hand spared

explanation.why_correct: Compression as the nerve enters the hand affects all ulnar-innervated hand muscles. Because the lesion is proximal to the superficial terminal cutaneous branch but distal to the palmar and dorsal cutaneous branches, sensory loss occurs only on the distal palm and the palmar surfaces of the fifth finger and medial half of the fourth finger. The proximal palmar area and the entire dorsum of the hand are spared.
distractors: Loss on both palmar and dorsal surfaces extending to the wrist occurs when all three sensory branches are affected, as with lesions at or above the elbow.
The dorsum of the ulnar hand is supplied by the dorsal cutaneous branch, which arises above the wrist and is spared by this lesion.
Absent sensory loss occurs when the compression is distal to the superficial terminal cutaneous branch and affects only the motor branch, which is not the case here.
explanation.key_point: A lesion at the entrance to the hand spares the dorsum and proximal palm but causes palmar sensory loss in the distal ulnar territory.

section: Purely motor ulnar lesion in the hand
source_quote: Because the lesion is distal to the superficial terminal cutaneous branch, there is no sensory loss.
vignette: A 40-year-old cyclist has progressive wasting of the hypothenar eminence and interossei with weakness of finger abduction and thumb adduction. When he pulls on a sheet of paper held between thumb and index finger, the thumb interphalangeal joint flexes. Sensation is normal throughout the hand, including the palmar surface of the fifth finger and the dorsum.
question: Where is the lesion most likely located?
options: Ulnar nerve above the elbow (medial cord of the brachial plexus)
Median nerve within the carpal tunnel
Deep motor branch of the ulnar nerve within the canal of Guyon, distal to the superficial terminal sensory branch
Ulnar nerve entering the hand, proximal to the origin of the superficial terminal sensory branch

explanation.why_correct: Compression of the proximal part of the terminal motor branch within the canal of Guyon affects all the ulnar-innervated hand muscles, producing a purely motor lesion. Because it lies distal to the superficial terminal cutaneous branch, there is no sensory loss.
distractors: A lesion above the elbow affects all three ulnar sensory branches and produces sensory loss on the dorsal and palmar surfaces of the ulnar hand.
Carpal tunnel compression affects the median nerve (thenar muscles and median digits), not the ulnar-innervated interossei and hypothenar muscles.
Compression as the nerve enters the hand, proximal to the superficial terminal branch, would produce sensory loss on the distal palm and palmar fifth finger.
explanation.key_point: A purely motor ulnar syndrome with normal sensation points to the deep motor branch in the canal of Guyon.

source_quote: With these neuropathies, smaller diameter nerve fibers conveying pain and temperature sensation are preferentially involved.
vignette: A 62-year-old man with systemic amyloidosis reports burning feet. Examination shows markedly reduced pinprick and temperature perception in a stocking distribution, with relatively preserved vibration and joint position sense.
question: Which nerve fibers are preferentially involved?
options: Small-diameter fibers conveying pain and temperature
Large myelinated fibers conveying joint position sense and two-point discrimination
Anterior horn motor neurons
Dorsal column axons within the spinal cord

explanation.why_correct: In some polyneuropathies, including amyloid neuropathy, type I hereditary sensory neuropathy, Tangier disease, and some diabetic neuropathies, smaller diameter fibers conveying pain and temperature are preferentially involved, giving a dissociated sensory loss.
distractors: Selective loss of touch pressure, two-point discrimination, and joint position sense with spared pain and temperature (large myelinated fiber loss) occurs in Friedreich ataxia, vitamin B12 deficiency, and Guillain-Barre syndrome.
Anterior horn motor neuron involvement would cause weakness and atrophy, not a sensory dissociation.
Dorsal column involvement would impair vibration and position sense, which are relatively preserved here.
explanation.key_point: Amyloid and some diabetic neuropathies preferentially injure small fibers, so pain and temperature are lost with relative sparing of vibration and position sense.

source_quote: the proliferation of Mycobacterium leprae is greater in cooler tissues
vignette: A 38-year-old man with lepromatous leprosy has progressive loss of cutaneous sensation that began over the tip of the nose and the malar areas of the cheeks and later spread to other parts of the body.
question: What best explains this initial distribution of sensory loss?
options: Loss of the longest axons first, those farthest from the dorsal root ganglion
Greater proliferation of the causative mycobacterium in cooler tissues
Preferential involvement of large myelinated fibers
Preferential loss of the shortest axons, as in Tangier disease

explanation.why_correct: In lepromatous leprosy the progression of deficits is not determined by axonal length. Sensory loss occurs first over cooler body areas such as the tip of the nose and the malar areas of the cheeks, because proliferation of Mycobacterium leprae is greater in cooler tissues.
distractors: Length-dependent loss, in which the sites most distal from the dorsal root ganglion cells are affected first, is the pattern of many polyneuropathies such as diabetic polyneuropathy, not of leprosy.
Preferential involvement of large myelinated fibers would spare pain and temperature and cause loss of joint position and vibration, which does not match this temperature-related pattern.
In Tangier disease short axons are preferentially involved, so sensory loss starts proximally and progresses distally; this is a fiber-length mechanism, not the temperature mechanism of leprosy.
explanation.key_point: In lepromatous leprosy sensory loss begins in the coolest skin because the organism proliferates better there.

source_quote: The serratus anterior muscle fixes and stabilizes the scapula against the chest wall and is tested by observing for scapular winging
vignette: A 26-year-old man develops shoulder weakness and fatigue when raising his arm above his head after carrying a heavy backpack for several days. At rest the scapulae look normal, but when he pushes his outstretched arms against a wall the vertebral border of the right scapula stands away from the thorax. Pressing the right elbow backward against resistance with the hand on the hip is normal.
question: Which nerve is most likely injured?
options: Dorsal scapular nerve
Long thoracic nerve
Suprascapular nerve
Thoracodorsal nerve
Axillary nerve

explanation.why_correct: The long thoracic nerve supplies the serratus anterior, which fixes and stabilizes the scapula against the chest wall. Its paralysis causes a winged scapula that appears when the arm is pushed forward against resistance, and it is injured by pressure on the shoulder such as carrying heavy loads (rucksack paralysis).
distractors: The dorsal scapular nerve supplies the rhomboids, which are tested by pressing the elbow backward with the hand on the hip; this maneuver is normal here.
The suprascapular nerve supplies the supraspinatus and infraspinatus, producing weakness of abduction and external rotation rather than scapular winging.
The thoracodorsal nerve supplies the latissimus dorsi, with compromised arm adduction and little deformity.
The axillary nerve supplies the deltoid and teres minor, causing deltoid atrophy and difficulty abducting the arm, and an upper lateral arm sensory defect.
explanation.key_point: Winging of the scapula on pushing the arms forward indicates a long thoracic nerve lesion and serratus anterior weakness.

source_quote: This entrapment causes shoulder pain, which is aggravated by shoulder girdle movements, weakness, and eventual atrophy in the two spinati muscles.
vignette: A 29-year-old volleyball player has a deep, aching pain along the superior border of the right scapula, worse with shoulder girdle movements. Examination shows weakness of arm abduction and external rotation, with atrophy above and below the scapular spine. The deltoid is strong and sensation over the lateral upper arm is normal.
question: Which nerve and site of lesion best explain these findings?
options: Axillary nerve in the quadrilateral space
Dorsal scapular nerve within the scalenus medius muscle
Musculocutaneous nerve at the coracobrachialis muscle
Suprascapular nerve at the suprascapular notch
Long thoracic nerve over the first rib

explanation.why_correct: Entrapment of the suprascapular nerve in the suprascapular foramen causes shoulder pain aggravated by shoulder girdle movements, weakness, and eventual atrophy of the supraspinatus and infraspinatus. Supraspinatus paresis weakens arm abduction and infraspinatus paresis impairs external rotation.
distractors: The axillary nerve supplies the deltoid and teres minor and a sensory area over the upper lateral arm; the strong deltoid and normal sensation argue against it.
The dorsal scapular nerve supplies the rhomboids and levator scapulae, so its lesion causes rhomboid weakness and scapular displacement, not weak abduction and external rotation.
The musculocutaneous nerve supplies the coracobrachialis, biceps, and brachialis, causing elbow flexion weakness and loss of the biceps reflex.
The long thoracic nerve supplies the serratus anterior and causes a winged scapula, not spinati atrophy.
explanation.key_point: Pain with weakness and atrophy of supraspinatus and infraspinatus in an overhead athlete points to suprascapular nerve entrapment.

source_quote: thigh flexion is spared because of the more proximal origin of the femoral nerve branches to the iliacus and psoas muscles
vignette: A 33-year-old woman has weakness of knee extension, a depressed patellar reflex, and numbness of the anteromedial thigh and inner leg after a prolonged delivery in the lithotomy position, with her hips flexed, abducted, and externally rotated. Hip flexion strength is normal.
question: Where along the nerve is the lesion most likely located?
options: Within the psoas muscle or pelvis (for example, an iliopsoas hematoma)
In the adductor (Hunter) canal
At the inguinal ligament
Obturator canal
Femoral triangle, affecting only the posterior division beyond the saphenous branch

explanation.why_correct: Femoral neuropathy in the lithotomy position results from compression against the inguinal ligament or excessive stretch. Lesions at the inguinal ligament cause quadriceps weakness, a depressed patellar reflex, and anteromedial thigh and inner leg sensory loss, but thigh flexion is spared because the branches to the iliacus and psoas arise more proximally.
distractors: A proximal lesion within the lumbar plexus, pelvis, or psoas would also weaken hip flexion (iliacus, psoas, and rectus femoris), which is normal here.
A saphenous lesion in the adductor canal produces only sensory disturbance of the medial lower leg, without quadriceps weakness or a depressed patellar reflex.
The obturator nerve supplies the thigh adductors and the medial thigh skin; it does not cause knee extension weakness or a depressed patellar reflex.
A lesion of the posterior division distal to the saphenous branch causes purely motor quadriceps weakness without sensory loss, but this patient has sensory loss.
explanation.key_point: A femoral neuropathy at the inguinal ligament weakens the quadriceps but spares hip flexion.

source_quote: There is a decrease or absence of the Achilles reflex (S1-S2), which is served by the tibial nerve.
vignette: A 44-year-old man develops a foot drop after an intramuscular injection into the buttock. Examination shows weakness of ankle dorsiflexion, eversion, plantar flexion, and toe flexion, an absent Achilles reflex, and numbness of the dorsolateral foot and the sole. The skin of the medial lower leg has normal sensation.
question: Where is the lesion most likely located?
options: Common peroneal nerve at the fibular head
Tibial nerve in the popliteal fossa
Sciatic nerve in the gluteal region
Deep peroneal nerve at the ankle
Superficial peroneal nerve in the leg

explanation.why_correct: A high sciatic lesion causes paralysis of foot dorsiflexion and eversion (peroneal division) and of plantar flexion and toe flexion (tibial division), a decreased or absent Achilles reflex served by the tibial nerve, and sensory loss on the outer leg and dorsum of the foot together with the sole. The medial leg is spared because it is supplied by the saphenous nerve (a femoral branch). Injection injuries of the sciatic nerve are described in the buttock.
distractors: A common peroneal lesion at the fibular head weakens dorsiflexion and eversion but spares plantar flexion, toe flexion, and the Achilles reflex, and spares the sole.
A tibial nerve lesion in the popliteal fossa weakens plantar flexion and inversion and causes sole sensory loss, but would not cause foot drop and dorsolateral foot numbness.
A deep peroneal lesion at the ankle weakens only the extensor digitorum brevis and affects the web between the first and second toes.
A superficial peroneal lesion weakens the peronei (eversion) and causes sensory loss on the lateral lower leg and foot dorsum, but spares dorsiflexion and plantar flexion.
explanation.key_point: A high sciatic lesion combines peroneal and tibial deficits, including a lost Achilles reflex, and is easily mistaken for a peroneal neuropathy.

source_quote: Because the extensor carpi radialis is unaffected while the extensor carpi ulnaris is paretic, the wrist deviates radially
vignette: A 36-year-old orchestra conductor has gradual difficulty extending the fingers at the metacarpophalangeal joints and the thumb. When he makes a fist, the wrist deviates radially, but he can still extend the wrist. Sensation, brachioradialis strength, and triceps strength and reflex are normal.
question: Where is the radial nerve lesion most likely located?
options: Radial nerve in the spiral groove
Posterior interosseous nerve at the supinator
Radial nerve in the axilla
Superficial branch of the radial nerve
Posterior cord of the brachial plexus

explanation.why_correct: A posterior interosseous nerve lesion produces drop-finger deformity and difficulty extending the thumb and abducting it. Because the extensor carpi radialis is unaffected while the extensor carpi ulnaris is paretic, the wrist deviates radially on making a fist. The nerve is purely motor, and the superficial sensory branch of the radial nerve is often spared. Entrapment at the supinator (arcade of Frohse) and chronic repeated forearm movements in conductors and violinists are described causes.
distractors: A spiral groove lesion produces wrist drop with weak brachioradialis and extensor carpi radialis longus and numbness on the dorsum of the hand.
An axillary radial lesion also paralyzes the triceps, abolishes the triceps reflex, and causes sensory loss on the extensor surface of the arm.
A lesion of the superficial radial branch is purely sensory and does not cause finger extensor weakness.
A posterior cord lesion would affect the axillary nerve and other posterior cord branches, with deltoid and triceps involvement.
explanation.key_point: Finger drop with radial wrist deviation and no sensory loss indicates a posterior interosseous nerve lesion.
